defects.name: Worn nosings
symptoms: Rounded or chipped front edge on treads
Splintering along the leading edge of the tread
Faded or worn finish concentrated at the nosing
Reduced grip underfoot at the step edge
causes: Cumulative foot traffic over years — softer timbers wear faster
Grit brought in on shoes acting as an abrasive
Original finish worn through, exposing bare timber
fixes: Light wear — sand back the nosing radius, reseal with matching finish
Moderate wear on softwood — nosing capping (a hardwood cover strip glued and pinned over the worn edge)
Severe wear or split — replace the tread or fit a full replacement nosing routed to match the string groove
vision_hints: Concentrated wear pattern on the front edge of treads
Visible colour change or bare timber at nosing
Chips or missing corners along the tread front

defects.name: Loose newel post
symptoms: Newel visibly moves side-to-side when the handrail is pushed
Gap opening at the base of the newel where it meets floor or bottom step
Handrail feels 'live' rather than solid when leant on
Creaking from newel joint under load
causes: Failed newel bolt through the string (most common)
Split or crushed timber at the newel-to-string joint
Original short-fixings where a full-length newel bolt was needed
Base fixings worked loose over years of use
fixes: Replace newel bolt with a longer/larger diameter through-bolt if the joint allows
If timber split, cut back to sound timber, glue and clamp, and re-bolt through fresh timber
For base-fixing failure, drill deeper anchors into the substrate (masonry or subfloor as appropriate)
vision_hints: Visible gap at newel base
Rotation marks or scoring at newel-to-string joint
Splintering or crushing at bolt location

evidence.source: General UK trade practice · interim-Author interpretation · verify with founding Author
Approved Document K · §2.3 (barrier loading requirements — a loose newel compromises balustrade compliance)

defects.name: Split string
symptoms: Visible crack running along the length of the string
Movement between the string and adjacent treads/risers
Widening gap between string and wall (wall string) or between string and newel (outer string)
Creaking or cracking sounds when the stair is used
causes: Overloading (heavy furniture moves, structural settlement)
Original timber knot or grain defect propagating with age
Damp cycling causing repeated expansion/contraction
Failed structural fixing above (e.g. loose trimmer) transferring load into the string
fixes: Surface crack: rout out, glue and clamp, splice-fit a repair patch, refinish
Deep crack through string thickness: reinforce with a steel or hardwood plate bolted through, then cosmetic repair
Severe or full-length split affecting the tread housings: replace the string (major job, often requires stair removal)
vision_hints: Linear crack visible on inside or outside face of string
Widening gap at ends of crack
Rust staining if steel fixings inside the crack

evidence.source: General UK trade practice · interim-Author interpretation · verify with founding Author

defects.name: Handrail loose at bracket or newel
symptoms: Handrail moves visibly when pushed sideways or downward
Gap opening between handrail and its fixing point
Rotation of the handrail around its long axis
Handrail no longer provides a secure grip when needed for support
causes: Bracket screws worked loose in the wall or newel
Wall plug failure (common in plasterboard fixings without proper anchors)
Handrail-to-newel joint (rebate or scarf) has opened up
Handrail-to-bracket connection screws stripped
fixes: Wall bracket loose: remove, upsize the fixings, use appropriate wall plugs (metal cavity anchors for plasterboard, expanding wall plugs for masonry)
Newel joint loose: strip back, re-glue with structural adhesive, add a concealed dowel or pocket screw
Bracket stripped: relocate the bracket 100-200mm along the rail into sound timber and infill/refinish the original hole
vision_hints: Bracket rotation or misalignment
Cracks in wall plaster around bracket fixings
Gap between handrail and its receiving joint

evidence.source: Approved Document K · §1.34-1.36 (handrails)

defects.name: Balustrade movement under load
symptoms: Whole balustrade rocks when pushed at the top rail
Visible flex in individual spindles under lateral pressure
Failure of the balustrade to feel solid — occupants avoid leaning on it
Rattle at the top or bottom of spindles when the balustrade is loaded
causes: Insufficient fixing between handrail/top rail and newel
Loose or missing spindle-to-string fixings
Failed adhesive-only spindle fixings (adhesive-only is not adequate for balustrade loading)
Undersized handrail cross-section for the span between newels
fixes: Add fixings at every spindle top and bottom (concealed dowel + adhesive, or pocket screw)
Reinforce handrail-to-newel joint with additional through-fixings
For undersized handrail: replace with a larger cross-section rated for domestic barrier loading (0.36 kN/m horizontal)
In severe cases: strip and rebuild the balustrade to current guarding compliance
vision_hints: Visible movement of balustrade under camera-tracked push test
Adhesive residue around spindle bases (indicates adhesive-only fixing)
Cracks or gaps at handrail-to-newel joint

defects.name: Spindle rattle in top or bottom rail
symptoms: Audible rattle from one or more spindles when the stair is walked or the balustrade is touched
Slight rotational movement of the spindle in its housing
Gap visible around the top or bottom of the spindle where it enters the rail
causes: Timber shrinkage — the spindle diameter has reduced slightly, leaving it loose in its socket
Failed adhesive at spindle housing
Original loose fit that was masked by fresh finish but has since worked loose
fixes: Remove spindle (lift out of top rail groove and out of bottom rail housing), clean the joint, re-glue with a wood glue that fills the joint (PVA + sawdust of the same timber, or a gap-filling PU adhesive)
For persistent looseness: wrap a thin sliver of matching veneer around the spindle end to take up the gap before re-fitting
Multiple rattling spindles across a run: consider environmental cause (heating change, humidity) — treat all at once
vision_hints: Gap visible around spindle where it meets the rail
Slight tilt off vertical when spindle is loose
Concentric ring of dust around loose spindle base

defects.name: Damp-rotted string end
symptoms: Softening or discolouration of the string at the bottom, particularly where it meets masonry or concrete floor
Timber crumbles when pressed with a screwdriver point
Visible fungal growth or musty smell at the string end
Loss of finish + darkening of timber near the affected area
causes: Rising damp through the substrate the string sits on
Water ingress from an external door or window not far from the stair
Poor ventilation to a closed-in understair void
Prolonged spillage or standing water at the bottom step
fixes: Identify and stop the moisture source first — repairing rotted timber over ongoing damp will fail
Cut back the rotted section to sound timber (typically 100-200mm past visible rot)
Splice a new hardwood section into the string with a scarf joint (typically 4:1 ratio) glued and mechanically fixed
Refinish the repaired section and consider a moisture-resistant coating for the ground-level portion
vision_hints: Colour change at string base
Visible fungal growth (white, black, or brown surface deposits)
Deformation or sag of the bottom of the string

evidence.source: General UK trade practice · interim-Author interpretation · verify with founding Author

defects.name: Separately-fitted nosing detaching
symptoms: Visible gap between the nosing profile and the front edge of the tread
Movement of the nosing when pressed
Nosing comes away when someone catches it with a foot
causes: Adhesive-only fixing has failed with age or moisture
Original nail or pin fixings have worked loose
Impact damage (heavy object dropped, foot catch)
fixes: Remove the nosing completely — do not try to force it back into place over old adhesive
Clean the mating surfaces down to bare timber on both nosing and tread
Refit with a modern PU or hybrid adhesive AND mechanical fixings (pinned from the top with matching-timber plugs, or screwed through the top with counterbored plugs)
If the nosing itself is damaged: fabricate or purchase a matching replacement
vision_hints: Visible gap under the nosing edge
Nosing tilted forward or downward
Adhesive residue visible on removed nosing

defects.name: Broken or cracked tread
symptoms: Visible crack across the tread width
Tread flexes or gives underfoot at the crack line
Splintering or missing material at the crack
Audible crack sound when the tread is loaded
causes: Undersized tread thickness for the span (older stairs with slim treads on wide flights)
Grain defect or knot in the original timber that has propagated
Impact damage (heavy furniture drop, blow from a hard object)
Damp cycle fatigue on external or damp-exposed stairs
fixes: Immediate — block off the stair to prevent use until repair is complete
Assess whether the tread can be repaired (surface crack in sound thicker timber) or must be replaced (crack through the full thickness or wide flight)
Repair route: rout out crack, glue with structural adhesive, clamp, reinforce underside with a steel plate or timber batten if required
Replacement route: remove the tread from between the strings (may require partial string disassembly), fit a new matching tread
vision_hints: Linear crack across tread width
Sag or step in tread level compared to neighbouring treads
Splinters or missing chunks

evidence.source: General UK trade practice · interim-Author interpretation · verify with founding Author

defects.name: Excessive tread deflection
symptoms: Tread visibly bounces or dips under normal loading
Squeak accompanies the deflection
Deflection felt underfoot but no visible crack (yet)
Worse in the centre of wide-flight treads
causes: Tread material undersized for the span (common on wider stairs with softwood treads)
Timber has moved and lost stiffness with age or moisture cycling
Original design used a lighter grade than intended
Additional loading the stair wasn't designed for (heavy piano moves, safe installations upstairs)
fixes: Confirm the deflection is elastic (returns to level) and not permanent sag — permanent sag suggests structural fatigue and requires tread replacement
For elastic deflection: add support underneath — a mid-span carriage timber running under the treads, or an additional string reinforcement
For permanent sag or repeated deflection: replace with thicker or higher-grade timber tread material
vision_hints: Sag visible when tread is unloaded (edge alignment across the flight)
Bounce visible in slow-motion video of stair use
Concentrated wear pattern in the centre of the tread

evidence.source: General UK trade practice · interim-Author interpretation · verify with founding Author

defects.name: Insufficient balustrade height (regulation gap)
symptoms: Handrail or top rail measures less than 900mm above the pitch line (private dwelling) or less than 1100mm above the floor (other building types or balconies)
Homeowners feel the balustrade is 'too low' to lean on comfortably
Building control flags the balustrade during renovation approval
causes: Stair predates the current Approved Doc K height requirements
Original design met a superseded regulation
Non-compliant retrofit — someone shortened the balustrade for aesthetic reasons
fixes: Extend the existing balustrade upward with a matching top-rail addition, or replace with a taller balustrade
For a single-family home, minor breaches may be tolerated by building control if the stair is not being altered — but any major renovation triggers current regs
Where the balustrade shape must be preserved (heritage property), consult a conservation officer before altering
vision_hints: Handrail visibly at hip-height rather than at low-torso height
Occupants photographed leaning over the rail

evidence.source: Approved Document K · §2.1 (guarding heights)

defects.name: Spindle gaps exceeding the 100mm sphere rule
symptoms: Gaps between spindles, between end spindles and newels, or between horizontal rails greater than 100mm
A 100mm-diameter ball, disc or child's head can pass through the gap
causes: Stair predates the current Approved Doc K guarding requirements
Missing spindles never replaced
Aesthetic 'minimalist' balustrade that ignored the 100mm rule
Original design used horizontal spacing greater than 100mm
fixes: Add additional spindles to close each gap below 100mm — usually 100mm centre-to-centre spacing works for standard-diameter spindles
For missing individual spindles: replace like-for-like
For heritage properties where original spindle count cannot be added to: seek conservation officer approval for a discrete infill (e.g. glass panel behind original balustrade)
vision_hints: Wide visible gaps between vertical members
Missing spindles
Horizontal-rail-only balustrades (a ladder pattern children can climb)

evidence.source: Approved Document K · §2.4 (100mm sphere rule)

defects.name: Cupped or twisted treads
symptoms: Tread surface is no longer flat — hollowed across width (cupping) or one corner high (twist)
Uneven wear pattern on the finished surface
Slight instability underfoot
Visible when a straight edge is laid across the tread
causes: Moisture imbalance between top and bottom faces of the tread — the drier face pulls into a curve
Original tread cut with pith or reaction wood present
One side finished, the other side bare timber — different vapour exchange rates
Environmental humidity swings, particularly with underfloor heating fitted after the stair
fixes: For minor cupping: sand back the high edges and refinish (accept some loss of tread thickness)
For moderate cupping/twist: remove the tread, allow to acclimatise flat and weighted for 2-4 weeks in the target environment, refit if it flattens; discard if not
For solid timber replacements: prefer quarter-sawn or engineered treads which are far more dimensionally stable
Address environmental cause if identified (balance humidity, seal underside)
vision_hints: Visible curve across tread width when a straight edge is placed
Uneven finish sheen (dips catch light differently)
Gap between straight edge and tread surface at the centre or corner

evidence.source: General UK trade practice · interim-Author interpretation · verify with founding Author

defects.name: Gap between tread and riser
symptoms: Visible daylight or dust-line where the tread meets the riser at the back of the tread
Debris and grit accumulating in the gap
Squeaking accompanies loading in some cases
The gap appears seasonally (opens in dry heated periods, closes in damp)
causes: Original joint (usually a housing or a butt with adhesive + pin) has failed
Timber shrinkage over years or from a heating change
Failed angle blocks behind the joint contributing to movement
Poor original assembly — insufficient adhesive or missing pin
fixes: Small cosmetic gap: fill with matching coloured wood filler + touch up finish
Moderate gap with movement: reinforce from behind if access — add or replace angle blocks, add adhesive to the joint
Significant gap with structural movement: strip the tread, clean the joint, re-fit with fresh adhesive and mechanical fixings
vision_hints: Fine gap visible at the back of the tread
Dust deposit line at the joint
Slight vertical misalignment between tread rear and riser top

evidence.source: General UK trade practice · interim-Author interpretation · verify with founding Author

defects.name: Flaking paint or failed varnish on stair components
symptoms: Paint peeling in strips or flakes, particularly at nosings and tread edges
Varnish clouding, cracking or lifting from the timber
Rough patchy finish where fresh timber is exposed under failed coating
Sticky or gummy feel to old varnish that hasn't cured properly
causes: Incompatible coats — oil-based over water-based or vice versa without a proper primer
Applied to timber that was too wet or too dry, or to a contaminated surface
UV degradation — varnish on a sunlit stair breaks down faster than on a shaded one
Foot traffic wearing through the finish, then moisture ingress lifting the surrounding intact area
fixes: Strip fully back to bare timber (mechanical sanding or chemical stripper depending on scale)
Assess the underlying timber — repair any splits, worn nosings or damaged edges before refinishing
Apply an appropriate primer + top coat system rated for high-traffic stair treads (typically 2K polyurethane or high-solids polish)
Do not refinish over failing coatings — the new coat will fail with the old
vision_hints: Flake pattern along tread edges
Colour change or bare timber visible under lifted finish
Sheen mismatch where finish has been touched up unsuccessfully

evidence.source: General UK trade practice · interim-Author interpretation · verify with founding Author
